Abstract # Birkhoff and Pierce asked in 1956 whether C\mathbb{C}C admits a lattice order compatible with the ring operations. The question was answered in the affirmative in 2026, and the structural problem is now to locate the lattice cones among all directed partial orders. Using a transcendence basis of C\mathbb{C}C over Q\mathbb{Q}Q we embed C\mathbb{C}C into a field of Puiseux series F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}} and stratify the directed partial orders by how much of the expansion a rule has to read: five nested conditions A⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒EA \Rightarrow B \Rightarrow C \Rightarrow D \Rightarrow EA⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒E, and six types. A cone satisfying CCC is never a lattice order, so no lattice cone is of Type 1, 2 or 3; and no lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C has 111 as a strong unit, since a lattice-ordered field in which 111 is a strong unit embeds in R\mathbb{R}R, and R\mathbb{R}R has no square root of −1-1−1: the classical Archimedean argument therefore excludes nothing, and every lattice cone is of Type 4, 5 or 6. Type 4 contains lattice cones: the cones of He and of Bao and Zhang are of this type, and so is a cone constructed here from their recursion with a different seed, in which 111 is not positive. Type 6 is not void in the wider class of lattice-ordered fields—Q(2)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})Q(2​) with the cone {a+b2:a,b≥0}\{a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \ge 0\}{a+b2​:a,b≥0} is one—but no cone of Type 5 or of Type 6 on C\mathbb{C}C is known. The group of order units separates the two families: it equals Q>0\mathbb{Q}_{>0}Q>0​ on the cones of Bao and Zhang and is uncountable on the basic order DDD.
Keywords: directed partial order, Puiseux series, valuation, lattice-ordered field, Birkhoff–Pierce problem
MSC 2020: 06F25 (primary); 12J15, 12J20 (secondary)
1. Introduction # In 1956, Birkhoff and Pierce asked whether the complex field C\mathbb{C}C admits a lattice order compatible with the ring operations [1]. In 2011, Schwartz and Yang proved that C\mathbb{C}C admits directed partial orders [2], that is, cones PPP with P−P=CP - P = \mathbb{C}P−P=C in the terminology of Definition 2.1, and they later showed that a field admits one if and only if it has characteristic 0 and is either real or of transcendence degree at least 1 over Q\mathbb{Q}Q [3]. For a non-Archimedean totally ordered field FFF, the directed partial orders on F(i)F(i)F(i) compatible with the order of FFF were studied by Rump and Yang [4], by Ma, Wu and Zhang [5, 6, 7], and by Xu and Zhang [8]; Wang, Yuan, Zhang and Zhu [9] added a construction by integral closures of local rings and conjectured that no lattice order exists on C\mathbb{C}C. None of these orders is a lattice order.
That conjecture was refuted by [10, 11], which answered the Birkhoff–Pierce question in the affirmative. In [10], He constructs, for every real t>1t > 1t>1 transcendental over Q\mathbb{Q}Q, a compatible lattice order on C\mathbb{C}C with 0≺10 \prec 10≺1, 0∨i=t0 \vee i = t0∨i=t and 1∧t=01 \wedge t = 01∧t=0, and obtains at least 2ℵ02^{\aleph_0}2ℵ0​ distinct lattice orders, each extending the usual order on Q\mathbb{Q}Q. In [11], Bao and Zhang construct a lattice positive cone PPP from a valuation of value group Q\mathbb{Q}Q and a transfinite recursion of countable ordinal length, with 1∈P1 \in P1∈P, Q>0⊆P\mathbb{Q}_{>0} \subseteq PQ>0​⊆P, P∩Q=Q≥0P \cap \mathbb{Q} = \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}P∩Q=Q≥0​, {x∈P×:x−1∈P}=Q>0\{x \in P^{\times} : x^{-1} \in P\} = \mathbb{Q}_{>0}{x∈P×:x−1∈P}=Q>0​, 0∨i=(t+i)/20 \vee i = (t + i)/20∨i=(t+i)/2 and 0∨(−i)=(t−i)/20 \vee (-i) = (t - i)/20∨(−i)=(t−i)/2, and they show that there are exactly 2c2^{\mathfrak{c}}2c lattice positive cones on C\mathbb{C}C, where c=∣C∣\mathfrak{c} = |\mathbb{C}|c=∣C∣. The existence problem is therefore closed, and the questions that remain are structural: which cones are lattice cones, how the new examples relate to the cones of [2]–[9], and which property of a cone forbids the suprema that a lattice order has to possess.
This paper answers the last question inside a hierarchy. Section 3 constructs directed partial orders from a Puiseux expansion of the complex numbers, without assuming an ordered subfield in advance. Section 4 stratifies all directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C by how much of that expansion a rule has to read, and obtains five nested conditions A⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒EA \Rightarrow B \Rightarrow C \Rightarrow D \Rightarrow EA⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒E together with six types. The central result there is Theorem 4.13: a cone that is insensitive to all the small changes of some pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a) is never a lattice order, so Types 1, 2 and 3 contain no lattice cone. Section 5 supplies the other half. Type 6 is the Archimedean case, and a lattice-ordered field in which 111 is a strong unit embeds in R\mathbb{R}R, which C\mathbb{C}C cannot do: 111 is therefore a strong unit of no lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C, and every lattice cone whatsoever is of Type 4, 5 or 6 (Theorem 5.13). Both cones of [10] and [11] are lattice cones, so by Theorem 4.13 neither of them satisfies condition CCC; §5.2 records the construction of [11] and locates it in Type 4, §5.4 runs the same recursion from a different seed, which gives a lattice cone with 1∉P1 \notin P1∈/P, and §5.3 locates the cone of [10], which is of Type 4 as well.
The contributions can be listed at once. (i) A Puiseux expansion of C\mathbb{C}C that presupposes no ordered subfield, and the cones d(S)d(S)d(S) read off from it (§3). (ii) The stratification itself: five nested conditions and six types, the Covering Lemma, a complete description of the cones of bounded depth as cards satisfying a product and a sum condition, and the theorem that a cone satisfying condition CCC is never a lattice order (§4). (iii) The location of the lattice cones: Types 1–3 are forbidden, 111 is a strong unit of none of them, so the classical Archimedean argument excludes nothing, and the three lattice cones whose type can be computed, namely those of He, those of Bao and Zhang, and a cone with 1∉P1 \notin P1∈/P obtained by running the recursion of Bao and Zhang from a second seed, are all of Type 4 (§5). (iv) Two invariants, the unit interval and the group of order units, which separate the known lattice cones from every cone constructed here without reference to an expansion (§5.8).
The stratification thus explains, after the fact, why seventy years of constructions produced no lattice order: each of them reads one term of a series, or a window of fixed width, or the small changes of a single pair, and all of them fall into Types 1–3. It also matches the shape of the affirmative answers, which prescribe the supremum of the incomparable pair 0,i0, i0,i explicitly: a cone that reads a bounded part of an expansion cannot do that, and by Theorem 4.13 no cone of Types 1–3 prescribes it.
Two limitations must be stated at the outset. First, the structural theorems of Section 4 are relative to the level valuation: condition AAA allows an arbitrary nontrivial valuation of C\mathbb{C}C, whereas Theorems 4.5–4.8 describe the cones of bounded depth only for the valuation given by the fixed expansion. Second, we do not decide when two choices of the transcendence basis, of the transcendental element and of the embedding give the same cone; no equivalence criterion is known to us, and we record the question as an open problem in Section 5.

Let K⊆LK \subseteq LK⊆L be fields. We use two standard facts: the elements of an algebraically closed field that are algebraic over a given subfield form an algebraically closed subfield, and if LLL is algebraic over KKK, then every embedding of KKK into an algebraically closed field extends to an embedding of LLL. Three requirements determine the choice of the variable and of the coefficients. First, the variable ttt must be transcendental over the field FFF of coefficients. Second, FFF must be algebraically closed, by the Newton–Puiseux Theorem 2.1. Third, FFF must be large enough that every complex number is algebraic over F(t)F(t)F(t), so that all of C\mathbb{C}C sits inside the series field. A transcendence basis TTT meets all three requirements at once. We fix a transcendence basis TTT of C\mathbb{C}C over Q\mathbb{Q}Q and one element t∈Tt \in Tt∈T. Newton computed the expansion of an algebraic function in fractional powers of the variable by the method of the polygon, and the theorem is named after the proof of Puiseux [12]; a modern account of the theorem and of its place in ramification theory is [20, Ch. 2]. 3. Complex Numbers with Puiseux Series # In this section we write every complex number as a series and construct the basic directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C. There are three steps: we isolate one transcendental number ttt, we embed C\mathbb{C}C into a field of Puiseux series in s=1ts = \frac{1}{t}s=t1​, and we define positivity by a condition on the first coefficient.
Definition 3.1. The field of Puiseux series over kkk in sss is
k{{s}}=⋃n≥1k((s1/n)). k\{\{s\}\} = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} k\big((s^{1/n})\big). k{{s}}=n≥1⋃​k((s1/n)).Thus a nonzero Puiseux series is a formal sum ∑qcqsq\sum_q c_q s^q∑q​cq​sq with cq∈kc_q \in kcq​∈k, whose exponents qqq are rational numbers with a common denominator and are bounded below. Fractional exponents cannot be avoided: a square root of sss is not a Laurent series in sss.
Lemma 3.1. There is an embedding of fields ι:C→F{{s}}\iota: \mathbb{C} \to F\{\{s\}\}ι:C→F{{s}} which is the identity on FFF and sends ttt to s−1s^{-1}s−1.
Proof. The set of elements of C\mathbb{C}C that are algebraic over a subfield is an algebraically closed subfield, and it contains every number algebraic over Q\mathbb{Q}Q. If ttt were algebraic over FFF, it would be algebraic over Q(T∖{t})\mathbb{Q}(T \setminus \{t\})Q(T∖{t}), contradicting the algebraic independence of TTT. Thus FFF, which contains Q‾\overline{\mathbb{Q}}Q​, is an algebraically closed subfield of C\mathbb{C}C, and ttt is transcendental over FFF. Thus the isomorphism extends to an embedding of C\mathbb{C}C. □\square□

The embedding of Lemma 3.1 is a dictionary that translates each complex number into a series and preserves sums and products; after the translation the cone conditions become statements about adding and multiplying series.

3.2 Level, Leading Coefficient, and Normalized Series # A rule that reads the beginning of a series observes two things: where the series begins and with which coefficient. The first is the level, which measures the size of the number and takes the place of the absolute value; it is of no use by itself, since it does not come from an order on C\mathbb{C}C. The second is the leading coefficient.
Definition 3.2. Let z∈Cz \in \mathbb{C}z∈C be nonzero.

5.9 Open Problems # Three questions remain.
(Q1) Is Type 6 nonempty on C\mathbb{C}C? Equivalently, is there a directed partial order on C\mathbb{C}C with no nonzero relative infinitesimal? By Theorem 4.12 the condition is precisely that no nonzero element is infinitely small with respect to a positive one, for lattice cones the classical obstruction is absent: by Corollary 5.12 no lattice cone on C\mathbb{C}C has 1 as a strong unit, and Proposition 5.8 shows that the failure of boundedness is not exceptional, since 1 bounds no positive number at all. The type is not void: on Q(2)\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})Q(2​) the cone {a+b2:a,b≥0}\{a + b\sqrt{2} : a, b \ge 0\}{a+b2​:a,b≥0} is a lattice cone of Type 6, as noted after Lemma 5.11, and so is the coordinate cone of §5.3 on the countable field KKK, while the cone {0}∪[1,∞)\{0\} \cup [1, \infty){0}∪[1,∞) on Q\mathbb{Q}Q is of Type 6 without being a lattice. What is open is whether C\mathbb{C}C admits one. Lemma 5.5 supplies a sufficient condition, a Q\mathbb{Q}Q-basis of C\mathbb{C}C whose products have nonnegative rational coordinates, and no such basis is known; the constructions of §5 do not supply one, since the three lattice cones are of Type 4 and the ultrapower of a cone with 1∈P1 \in P1∈P always has a nonzero relative infinitesimal. The basis that [10, Theorem 5.1] builds on KKK is of exactly this kind, so the question is whether a positive basis on a countable subfield extends to one on C\mathbb{C}C; the obstruction is purely the passage to uncountable dimension, since a transfinite construction of length c\mathfrak{c}c would have to keep the structure constants nonnegative at limit stages. Formal realness is not the obstacle either: KKK contains iii and carries the lattice cone PKP_KPK​ with I(PK)={0}I(P_K) = \{0\}I(PK​)={0}.
Nor can an answer be modelled on the classical picture of Archimedean ordered fields, for no cone on C\mathbb{C}C is totally ordered, by Lemma 5.10 with Lemma 2.2: a Type 6 cone on C\mathbb{C}C would be a genuinely partial order without relative infinitesimals. Whether some cone of Type 6 on C\mathbb{C}C exists at all, and whether a lattice cone can be one, are both open.
(Q2) Is Type 5 nonempty? For lattice cones the question splits into two concrete conditions by Lemma 5.6: a lattice cone can escape Type 4 only if its monad is trivial or if 12∉P\frac{1}{2} \notin P21​∈/P, and each condition can be attacked separately. In general, by Remark 5.2, the question is whether some cone has relative infinitesimals while no pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a) preserves the positivity of a single one of its positive numbers. The three lattice cones whose type can be computed are of Type 4, so the expectation that the lattice cones are maximally sensitive is false as stated.
(Q3) When do two choices of (T,t,ι)(T, t, \iota)(T,t,ι) and of the cone SSS on the constants give the same cone? No equivalence criterion is known to us, and without one the description of Types 1 and 2 in Section 4 counts cones with multiplicity, once for every expansion that describes them. A criterion of the shape of the one obtained in [9] for generators of cones from integral closures would turn the stratification into a classification.

「破茧」摄影展回顾 # 这次摄影展的主题是 「破茧」。
从一岁一枯荣的草木更替，到南半球地平线上一抹温柔的黄昏；从枝头小憩的宁静瞬间，到破土而出、绝处逢生的倔强——镜头一点点把我们带离日常，重新看见周遭那些常常被忽略的小世界。
下面是这次展览中的作品回顾：
一点感想 # 回头再看这一组作品，其实还带着点稚嫩的痕迹：构图未必都恰到好处，光线也有几处没能抓住最好的瞬间。但换个角度想，哪一次启程不是从这样的「做起来」开始的？
不必等到万事俱备再动手。先举起相机，先按下快门，先把那些打动自己的瞬间收进来——哪怕粗糙，哪怕生涩。多走几步，多拍几次，自然就会慢慢知道：什么值得留在画面里，什么应该放掉。
「破茧」不只是这组照片的名字，大概也是做任何一件事的样子：先做起来，再逐渐成熟。

Abstract # Birkhoff and Pierce asked in 1956 whether the complex field C\mathbb{C}C admits a lattice order compatible with the ring operations. Schwartz and Yang proved in 2011 that C\mathbb{C}C admits directed partial orders. We give a new construction that by using a transcendence basis of C\mathbb{C}C over Q\mathbb{Q}Q, we embed C\mathbb{C}C into a field of Puiseux series F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}}, so that every complex number acquires a series expansion, and we define positivity by a condition on the leading coefficient. Every directed partial order we construct is placed in a stratification by how much of the expansion a rule has to read. Reading one term, a window of fixed width, or a sensitivity condition on small changes, we obtain five nested conditions A⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒EA \Rightarrow B \Rightarrow C \Rightarrow D \Rightarrow EA⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒E and six types. Relative to the fixed level valuation, cones satisfying BBB correspond to the cards satisfying a product and a sum condition. Cones satisfying CCC are never lattice orders, which excludes Types 1, 2, 3. We give an example of Type 4 that is not a lattice order either. The existence of a lattice order on C\mathbb{C}C and the existence of orders of Types 5 and 6 still remain open. This is a stratification rather than a complete classification because only Types 1–4 are shown to be nonempty.
Keywords: directed partial order, cone, Puiseux series, valuation, lattice-ordered ring, Birkhoff–Pierce problem
1. Introduction # In 1956, Birkhoff and Pierce asked the question whether the complex field C\mathbb{C}C admits a lattice order compatible under the rings [1]; in 2011, Schwartz and Yang proved that the directed partial order are admitted on C\mathbb{C}C [2] and later found that a field admits one if and only if it has characteristic 0 and is real or has the transcendence degree at least 1 over Q\mathbb{Q}Q [3]. Furthermore, for a non-archimedean totally ordered field FFF, the directed partial orders on F(i)F(i)F(i) compatible with the order of FFF were studied and classified by Rump and Yang [4], Ma, Wu, and Zhang [5] [6] [7], and Xu and Zhang [8]. Recently, Wang, Yuan, Zhang, and Zhu [9] also give a related example by construction, stating the conjecture that there does not exist lattice order on the complex field. None of these orders is a lattice order. However, He [10] gives a certain answer that C\mathbb{C}C admits at least 2ℵ02^{\aleph_0}2ℵ0​ distinct compatible lattice orders.
This paper has two parts. The first part is a direct construction on C\mathbb{C}C as an abstract field without ordered subfield given in advance. We write C\mathbb{C}C as the algebraic closure of F(t)F(t)F(t), where ttt is transcendental and FFF is an algebraically closed subfield, put s=1/ts = 1/ts=1/t, and embed C\mathbb{C}C into the field of Puiseux series over FFF in sss. Thus, every complex number becomes a series like a decimal expansion. The second part constructs a stratification to sort all directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C. We sort the orders by how much of the series must be read. With the restriction, we introduce five nested conditions and show every cone falls into one of the six classes exactly. The first four classes are proved and described to be nonempty, but the last two still remain some possibilities for their existence. The conditions are shaped by relative infinitesimals, the pairs of ring and ideal, and the leading coefficients. However, some of the types have no example and are unknown for the existence of the lattice order. The Birkhoff-Pierce problem still remains open in this paper.
Section 2 includes the necessary concepts and terms that ones need to know for the paper. Section 3 constructs the Puiseux expansion of complex numbers and the basic orders, proving the basic orders. Section 4 defines the six types of the stratification of the directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C, demonstrating the Covering Lemma and explaining each type of directed partial order.
2. Preliminaries # The purpose of this section is to mention some concepts and notations that appear in the proofs. For a subset III of C\mathbb{C}C, we write I×=I∖{0}I^{\times} = I \setminus \{0\}I×=I∖{0}. We define i=−1i = \sqrt{-1}i=−1​.
Let K⊆LK \subseteq LK⊆L be fields. We use two standard facts: the set of elements of an algebraically closed field that are algebraic over a given subfield is an algebraically closed subfield; if LLL is algebraic over KKK, then every embedding of KKK into an algebraically closed field extends to an embedding of LLL. When we decide the variable and the coefficients, three things guarantees the choice. First, the variable ttt must be transcendental over the field FFF of coefficients. Second, FFF must be algebraically closed because of the Newton-Puiseux Theorem 2.1. Third, FFF must be large enough in order that every complex number is algebraic over F(t)F(t)F(t) in order to let C\mathbb{C}C inside the series field. A transcendence basis TTT is the tool to achieve them at the same time. We fix a transcendence basis TTT of C\mathbb{C}C over Q\mathbb{Q}Q and one element t∈Tt \in Tt∈T. 3. Complex Numbers with Puiseux Series # In this section, we rewrite every complex number as the form of series and construct the basic directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C. There are three steps: we isolate one transcendental number ttt, embed C\mathbb{C}C into a field of Puiseux series in s=1ts = \frac{1}{t}s=t1​, and define positivity by a condition on the first coefficient.
Definition 3.1. The field of Puiseux series over kkk in sss is
k{{s}}=⋃n≥1k((s1/n)). k\{\{s\}\} = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} k\big((s^{1/n})\big). k{{s}}=n≥1⋃​k((s1/n)).Thus, a nonzero Puiseux series is a formal sum ∑qcqsq\sum_q c_q s^q∑q​cq​sq with cq∈kc_q \in kcq​∈k, whose exponents qqq are rational numbers with a common denominator and are bounded below. Lemma 3.1. There is an embedding of fields ι:C→F{{s}}\iota: \mathbb{C} \to F\{\{s\}\}ι:C→F{{s}} which is the identity on FFF and sends ttt to s−1s^{-1}s−1.
Proof. The set of elements of C\mathbb{C}C that are algebraic over a subfield is an algebraically closed subfield, and it contains every number algebraic over Q\mathbb{Q}Q. If ttt were algebraic over FFF, it would be algebraic over Q(T∖{t})\mathbb{Q}(T \setminus \{t\})Q(T∖{t}), contradicting the algebraic independence of TTT. Thus, FFF which contains Q‾\overline{\mathbb{Q}}Q​ is an algebraically closed subfield of C\mathbb{C}C, and ttt is transcendental over FFF. Therefore, there is an isomorphism of F(t)F(t)F(t) onto the subfield F(s)F(s)F(s) of F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}} which is the identity on FFF and sends ttt to s−1s^{-1}s−1. Because every complex number is algebraic over Q(T)\mathbb{Q}(T)Q(T) and Q(T)⊆F(t)\mathbb{Q}(T) \subseteq F(t)Q(T)⊆F(t), every complex number is algebraic over F(t)=F(s)F(t) = F(s)F(t)=F(s). Abstract # Kuratowski’s Theorem identifies planar graphs by determining the existence of two forbidden subdivisions, K5K_5K5​ and K3,3K_{3,3}K3,3​. This paper provides an expansion of Thomassens’ proof with extra explanation, focusing on the method involved Menger’s Theorem and connectivity. It demonstrates certifying algorithm as the application of the theorem, illustrating a linear-time verification algorithm for non-planarity and presenting.
1. Introduction # Every student learning topological graph theory eventually hears about Kuratowski’s Theorem, which is one of the most-cited results in this rapidly growing subject [12]. The planar problem was first solved with two forbidden patterns by Kazimierz Kuratowski in 1930, so the theorem is named after him [13]. Planarity is the bridge which connects geometry and combinatorics. Specifically, Kuratowski’s Theorem can be cited as a starting point for planarity in topological graph theory. It simplifies the problem of whether a graph can be drawn without crossings into simple checking for two specific patterns K5K_5K5​ and K3,3K_{3,3}K3,3​.
This paper gives the proof of Thomassen’s modern approach, explaining how the theorem is applied to certifying algorithms by planarity testing and extraction in linear time, a tool in optimization. It is written as a lead-in in topological graph theory for beginners who grasp the basic definitions of graph theory.
For the rest of the paper, Section 2 is the preliminary section, which includes all the concepts and terms that ones need to know for the paper. Section 3 gives the proof of Menger’s Theorem, which is essential when proving Kuratowski’s Theorem, through the three cases with the classification of the place of the separator. Section 4 is where we prove Kuratowski’s Theorem with lemmas, based on the proof of Thomassen’s version. Section 5 is the place to show its adaptation in certifying algorithms, providing a future direction of the research.
2. Preliminaries # The purpose of this section is to mention some concepts and notations that appear in the proofs. Without stating explicitly, the graphs are in the Euclidean plane, and they are simple graph. Without citing specifically, the formal definitions all come from Graph Theory written by Diestel. [1] Assuming familiarity with basic terminologies in graph theory, we follow.
A non-empty graph GGG is connected if any two of the vertices are linked by a path in GGG. A vertex separating GGG is a cut-vertex. The graph GGG is kkk-connected if ∣G∣>k|G| > k∣G∣>k and G−XG-XG−X are connected, for every set X≤VX \le VX≤V with ∣X∣<k|X| < k∣X∣<k. An edge e∈Ee \in Ee∈E is called a bridge if the graph Ge={V,E∖e}G_e = \{V,E\setminus e\}Ge​={V,E∖e} is disconnected. A separator is the set of vertices whose removal leaves no path between its endpoints. The cyclic order of a set of internally disjoint u−vu-vu−v paths around an endpoint is the clockwise sequence in which these paths intersect a small circle centered at the endpoint. Two such orders are identical if they are different only by rotation, and opposite if one is the rotation of the reverse of the other.
A plane graph is a pair of {V,E}\{V,E\}{V,E} of finite sets with the properties: V⊆R2V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2V⊆R2; every edge has its own set of endpoints; the interior of an edge does not contain a vertex or point of any other edge. Comprehensively, a graph is planar if it can be drawn in such a way that pairs of edges intersect only at vertices. A planar embedding is the way to draw a graph without edges passing through a vertex other than its own two endpoints, and edges do not cross with each other.
Euler’s formula provides both the necessary and sufficient foundation for the planarity of a finite graph.
Theorem 2.1 (Euler’s Theorem). Let GGG be a connected planar graph with vvv vertices, eee edges, and fff faces. Then, v−e+f=2v-e+f=2v−e+f=2.
Proof. By using induction on eee: If e=0e=0e=0, then the graph only has one vertex and one face. This base case is valid. Assume the equation holds for all planar graphs whose number of edges is less than eee. Let GGG be the graph with eee edges. If GGG is a tree, then v−e+f=v−(v−1)+1=2v-e+f=v-(v-1)+1=2v−e+f=v−(v−1)+1=2. If GGG is not a tree and has a cycle CCC which involves an edge eCe_CeC​, we consider the graph G−eCG-e_CG−eC​, which has the same number of vertices but one fewer edge and face. By the assumption, v−e+f=v−(e−1)+(f−1)=2v-e+f=v-(e-1)+(f-1)=2v−e+f=v−(e−1)+(f−1)=2. Thus, for the planar graphs, we have v−e+f=2v-e+f=2v−e+f=2. [2] □\square□
A straight line segment is a subset of R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 with the form {m+λ(m−n)∣λ∈[0,1]}\{m+\lambda(m-n)\mid\lambda\in[0,1]\}{m+λ(m−n)∣λ∈[0,1]} for distinct points m,n∈R2m,n\in\mathbb{R}^2m,n∈R2. An arc is the union of finitely many straight line segments. If PPP is an arc between xxx and yyy, we denote the point set P∖{x,y}P\setminus\{x,y\}P∖{x,y}. The frontier of a set X⊆R2X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2X⊆R2 is the set YYY of all points y∈R2y\in\mathbb{R}^2y∈R2.
Theorem 2.2 (Jordan Curve Theorem). For every polygon P⊆R2P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2P⊆R2, the set R2∖P\mathbb{R}^2\setminus PR2∖P has exactly two faces. Each of these has the entire polygon PPP as its frontier.
We take it as a known theorem, and we will not prove this theorem because it requires lots of topological definitions which we do not provide here. However, one can find some references like Algebraic Topology written by Allen Hatcher to help one understand this theorem. For our purposes, we will use its consequences that in a planar embedding, a cycle separates the plane into two parts with an inside and outside. Also, a set of three internally disjoint u−vu-vu−v paths will partition the plane into three faces.
Let HHH be a fixed graph. For an edge e=uv∈Ee=uv\in Ee=uv∈E with u≠vu\ne vu=v, the contraction graph G/eG/eG/e is defined: removing u,vu,vu,v, and add www, and redirect every edge incident to uuu or vvv (not eee) to www, and remove eee. Proof. Assume GGG contains a subdivision of XXX. We assume a subgraph H⊆GH\subseteq GH⊆G that is isomorphic to a subdivision of XXX. Each edge of XXX corresponds to a path in HHH. We contract each path into an edge with the length of 1. The result is XXX, and we have X⪯GX\preceq GX⪯G because contraction produces minors. □\square□

Proposition 2.4. After removing or contracting the edges, the planar graph is still planar.
Proof. We assume there is a planar embedding of GGG. Removing an edge eee does not cause the appearance of new crossings, so G−eG-eG−e is planar.
For the contraction, let uv∈E(G)uv\in E(G)uv∈E(G) be the edge to contract. The arc uvuvuv has no intersection, and we slide uuu along the arc uvuvuv to vvv by dragging all incident edges with it. 3. Menger’s Theorem # Menger’s Theorem, proved by Karl Menger in 1927, illustrates the connectivity of a graph not only by its separators but also by its paths, which makes it ”one of the cornerstones of graph theory.” [1] In this chapter, by discussing cases through lemmas, we will prove the theorem which contributes to our proof of Kuratowski’s Theorem by guaranteeing the internally disjoint u−vu-vu−v paths in GGG and determining the connected paths between the vertices as shown in Figure 2. It also provides the presence of disjoint paths which are needed to construct the forbidden subdivisions.
Menger’s Theorem: Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph and A,B⊆VA,B\subseteq VA,B⊆V. Then the minimum number of vertices separating AAA from BBB in GGG is equal to the maximum number of disjoint A−BA-BA−B paths in GGG.
Figure 2: A Visual Example of Menger’s Theorem

Let AAA and BBB be the vertices of GGG. Let p(G)p(G)p(G) denote the maximum of the number of internally disjoint A−BA-BA−B paths, and let q(G)q(G)q(G) denote the minimum of the size of an A−BA-BA−B vertex separator. There is the inequality p(G)≤q(G)p(G)\le q(G)p(G)≤q(G) because every path system uses at least one vertex from every separator. The first case is the normal one that the minimum separator locates somewhere in the middle of the graph, so we can cut the graph along the separator to produce two smaller pieces. Proof. Let SSS be the separator with ∣S∣=q(G)|S|=q(G)∣S∣=q(G). The graph GGG can be separated into subgraphs G1G_1G1​ and G2G_2G2​. 5. Application: Planarity Testing # When a graph is certified to be nonplanar, we should ensure both efficiency and accuracy. Kuratowski’s Theorem provides not only a simple testing method for planar graphs but also a foundation of algorithms in computational graph theory, illustrating an optimized way to find nonplanar graphs in a shorter period of time. There are two certifying algorithms determining planarity in linear time with the help of Kuratowski’s Theorem: Hopcroft-Tarjan algorithm and Boyer-Myrvold algorithm. In this section, we introduce how Kuratowski’s Theorem is involved in certifying verification algorithms, especially utilized in Hopcroft-Tarjan algorithm of planarity testing.

5.3 Hopcroft-Tarjan Algorithm # Hopcroft-Tarjan algorithm, introduced in 1974, was the first algorithm to test the planarity of a graph in linear time. Before the appearance of this algorithm, planarity testing algorithms were either exponential or required restrictive assumptions for the input graphs. Hopcroft-Tarjan algorithm established an improvement in efficiency in algorithmic graph theory by constructing an embedding of the input graph through a depth-first search tree. If the algorithm cannot complete the planar embedding because of a conflict, it declares that the graph is not planar. However, Kuratowski’s Theorem provides a theoretical guarantee that the conflict can always be resolved into a subdivision of K5K_5K5​ or K3,3K_{3,3}K3,3​. In addition, the extracted subgraphs can be verified independently by isomorphism, requiring Kuratowski’s Theorem as a certificate validation [14].
We prove its property of linear time to better demonstrate its efficiency and function. The Hopcroft-Tarjan algorithm runs in linear time by a combination of depth-first search and path addition structure. Thus, we first prove some lemmas that describe the time in each phase, and finally combine them to obtain the time of the Hopcroft-Tarjan algorithm.

The improvement of the Hopcroft-Tarjan algorithm is the Boyer-Myrvold algorithm, which simplifies planarity testing by using an addition approach on edges rather than vertex addition, maintaining a partial embedding and attempting to place each edge on the external face. If an edge cannot be placed, the algorithm leaves a Kuratowski subgraph. However, unlike the function in the Hopcroft-Tarjan algorithm, the Boyer-Myrvold algorithm isolates the Kuratowski subgraphs during the embedding process, which involves native extraction and minimality supported by Kuratowski’s Theorem [15].
5.4 Further Reading # For readers interested in the broader context of topological graph theory, the classic textbook is Graph Theory written by Diestel [1]. As an extension of Kuratowski’s Theorem, Robertson-Seymour Theorem demonstrates a generalization by the finite obstruction set applying in arbitrary surfaces where Kuratowski’s Theorem only makes sense for the sphere. A more advanced attempt at graphs embeddings on surfaces is given by Graphs on Surfaces [18] written by Mohar and Thomassen. This extends Kuratowski characterizations to higher dimensional surfaces and discusses the problem of crossing numbers. For the intersection of topological graph theory and algorithms, Combinatorial Optimization written by Schrijver [17] provides an extensive area of planarity in the context of polyhedral combinatorics, including the use of Kuratowski subgraphs as cutting planes for the maximum planar subgraph problem.
